summary:
We developed an interactive platform that helps mission teams find terrestrial analogues for locations on the Moon and Mars. Users select a point on a 3D globe, choose a testing objective, and receive ten ranked Earth candidates with coordinates, satellite imagery, and explanations.

Using open NASA LOLA and MOLA data alongside NOAA ETOPO 2022, the platform compares terrain shape, elevation range, regional slope, and roughness across more than 1.35 million eligible Earth locations. Objective-specific weights adapt the comparison to rover testing, astronaut training, landing sensors, excavation, or geological exploration. Exact SHAP explanations reveal how each criterion contributes to a recommendation, while separate environmental passports highlight differences in temperature and atmospheric conditions.

The project turns planetary and Earth datasets into an accessible, transparent tool for discovering potential testing grounds beyond familiar analogue sites. It supports early mission preparation while clearly identifying where finer-resolution data, expert assessment, and field verification are still needed.
details:
Our project is an interactive platform that helps exploration teams find Earth locations with terrain similar to a selected area on the Moon or Mars. Users choose a destination on a 3D globe, mark a location or enter coordinates, and select a testing objective. The platform returns ten ranked terrestrial candidates with coordinates, country labels, satellite imagery, terrain comparisons, and explanations.

The search combines open NASA LRO LOLA data for the Moon, NASA MGS MOLA data for Mars, and NOAA ETOPO 2022 data for Earth. Each location is represented by a nominal 10 × 10 km window containing 25 elevation samples. The system compares terrain shape, elevation range, fitted-plane slope, and detrended RMS roughness against more than 1.35 million eligible Earth windows. Profiles are centred around their own mean elevation and compared under four rotations, allowing similarly shaped landscapes to match despite differences in absolute elevation or orientation.

The comparison adapts to the intended experiment. Rover testing prioritises slope and roughness, while landing-sensor testing prioritises terrain shape and elevation variation. A weighted sum of squared, normalised differences produces the mismatch score: lower values indicate closer terrain matches. Regional water screening and a separate geographic allocation rule also influence the returned shortlist.

Explainability is a central feature. Exact SHAP contributions show how each criterion improves or worsens a candidate’s score relative to the average of the returned shortlist. Users can inspect both the reasons for a recommendation and its remaining mismatches. Separate environmental passports provide temperature and atmospheric context from NASA POWER, the Mars Climate Database, and LRO Diviner. Source periods, missing values, and differences between measurements and model outputs remain visible; environmental conditions do not enter the terrain ranking.

We developed the interface with TypeScript, Vue, Nuxt, and Three.js. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, and a persistent Node.js terrain-search worker. NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and Matplotlib supported data analysis and visualisation. We also trained a separate scikit-learn MiniBatchKMeans research prototype to investigate terrain types; the live platform uses the objective-weighted retrieval method described above. GitHub Actions and Docker support testing and deployment.

The project’s creativity lies in connecting an arbitrary planetary destination to an interpretable, task-specific Earth shortlist. It searches beyond a fixed catalogue of famous analogue sites and gives teams evidence they can examine when planning an experiment.

Our team considered spatial resolution, consistent units, correlated terrain descriptors, coordinate conventions, incomplete environmental coverage, and the distinction between regional resemblance and actual testing suitability. We checked terrain calculations against analytical surfaces and verified that SHAP contributions reconstruct the score. Fine obstacles, soil mechanics, vegetation, access, and field safety still require additional assessment.

The intended impact is to make early analogue-site screening more accessible and transparent, helping teams identify promising locations for detailed surveys and field testing before committing resources to an expedition.
